title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn represents a failure of the normal cardiopulmonary transition at birth, in which pulmonary vascular resistance remains abnormally elevated, and pulmonary blood flow remains reduced. This course reviews the pathophysiology of this condition, which leads to right-to-left shunting across fetal circulatory pathways and refractory hypoxemia that can range from mild respiratory distress to life-threatening respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, as well as its multiple contributing antenatal, perinatal, and postnatal factors, including lung parenchymal disease, abnormal pulmonary vascular development, maternal conditions, and congenital anomalies.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity outlines the physiology, classification, diagnosis, and evidence-based management of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, as early recognition and targeted management remain critical to reducing morbidity and mortality during the neonatal period. Participants will also gain an understanding of the risk factors, interpretation of clinical findings and diagnostic studies, the oxygenation index, and contemporary ventilatory, pharmacologic, and supportive strategies of this condition. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, performing the recommended evaluation, appropriately escalating care, including the roles of inhaled nitric oxide and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition to support timely, patient-centered decision-making in high-risk neonates.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Introduction
content: The placenta functions as the primary organ for gas exchange during fetal life, while the lungs must rapidly assume this function after birth. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn develops when the normal transition from intrauterine to extrauterine circulation fails, resulting in persistently elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and reduced pulmonary blood flow.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Introduction
content: Clinical manifestations range from mild respiratory distress to severe hypoxic respiratory failure that may require mechanical ventilation and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn represents a potentially life-threatening condition during the early neonatal period, requiring prompt recognition and timely initiation of appropriate supportive and therapeutic interventions by healthcare practitioners. [1]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Etiology
content: Persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn can occur due to several reasons. Lung parenchymal conditions such as meconium aspiration syndrome, pneumonia, respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), and sepsis contribute to persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn. [2] Other etiological factors associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn include oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, infants of diabetic mothers, in utero closure of the ductus arteriosus, and small and large for gestational age status. [3]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Etiology
content: Maternal risk factors, eg, obesity, diabetes, preeclampsia, chorioamnionitis, smoking, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), and NSAID use during pregnancy, can also contribute to the development of persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn. [4] [5] [6] Congenital anomalies (eg, transposition of great arteries and congenital diaphragmatic hernia) are also associated with persistent fetal circulation in the immediate neonatal period.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Epidemiology
content: The overall incidence of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn measures 1.8 per 1000 live births. [7] [8] Contrary to common assumptions, a higher incidence is observed among late preterm infants (5.4 per 1000 live births) than among term infants (1.6 per 1000 live births). [9]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Epidemiology
content: Mortality rates range from 7.6% to 10.7%, depending on disease severity. Male infants demonstrate a higher risk than female infants, with an adjusted risk ratio of 0.8 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.7 to 0.8. African American infants experience the highest risk, followed closely by Hispanic and Asian infants.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Pathophysiology
content: A high PVR relative to systemic vascular resistance is essential for a normal intrauterine fetal circulation. Fluid-filled alveoli and hypoxia-induced pulmonary vasoconstriction in the presence of circulating vasoconstrictors such as endothelin-1 and thromboxane maintain high PVR in the fetal phase. Conversely, circulating levels of vasodilators, eg, nitric oxide and prostaglandins, are low. [10] Pulmonary reactivity to vasodilators increases with increasing gestational age.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Pathophysiology
content: During the normal transition after birth, several events occur simultaneously, resulting in a smooth transition to extrauterine life. At birth, clamping the umbilical cord significantly raises the systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This increase, combined with the decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance that occurs with lung aeration, shifts blood flow through the heart and great vessels away from the right-to-left shunting pattern seen in the fetus. The increased partial pressure of oxygen and the initiation of ventilation also stimulate the production of vasodilators, eg, nitric oxide and prostacyclins; cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) mediate pulmonary vasodilation through endothelial nitric oxide. [11]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Pathophysiology
content: Cyclooxygenase is a rate-limiting enzyme that mediates the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostacyclin. COX-1 is expressed in the lung and is upregulated at term gestation. Prostacyclins increase cAMP levels, which in turn cause vasorelaxation by decreasing intracellular calcium concentration. Nitric oxide-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (NO-cGMP) and nitric oxide-cyclic adenosine monophosphate (NO-cAMP) pathways are extensively studied in the pathophysiology of persistent fetal circulation. [12] [13] Subsequent clinical studies supported the widely accepted use of inhaled nitric oxide therapy for persistent pulmonary hypertension in newborns. title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Pathophysiology
content: Maladaptation : Maladaptation is characterized by abnormal pulmonary vascular response in lung parenchymal disorders, eg, meconium aspiration syndrome. Underdeveloped vasculature : Decreased pulmonary vasculature, as seen in small-for-gestational-age or oligohydramnios, results in persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn. Idiopathic persistent pulmonary hypertension in the newborn : This type is likely due to excessive thickness of pulmonary vascular smooth muscle. Intravascular obstruction : Increased blood viscosity, as seen in neonatal polycythemia, may contribute to functional intravascular obstruction of pulmonary blood flow; hematocrits above 54% may also increase pulmonary vascular resistance. [14] Additionally, these categories can overlap in any given condition. [1]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Pathophysiology
content: High PVR decreases pulmonary blood flow, leading to ventilation-perfusion mismatch and right-to-left shunting across the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, resulting in refractory hypoxemia. Extra-cardiac shunting across a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) results in more than a 10% differential between preductal and postductal saturations. [15] Infants with persistent pulmonary hypertension are vulnerable to wide swings in oxygen saturation and increased right-to-left shunting with minimal stimulation and agitation.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- History and Physical
content: Infants commonly present within a few days after birth. Prenatal history obtained at the time of NICU admission should include maternal medical conditions and documented drug exposure. Clinicians should also review relevant prenatal and perinatal factors, including chorioamnionitis, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and perinatal asphyxia, as these conditions contribute to the development of persistent pulmonary hypertension. [16]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- History and Physical
content: Newborn assessment often occurs concurrently with resuscitation, particularly in settings (eg, meconium aspiration). A greater than 10% difference in oxygen saturation may be observed between preductal measurements obtained from the right upper extremity and postductal measurements obtained from a lower extremity. Normal, nondifferential preductal and postductal saturation values do not exclude persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, since shunting may also occur through the foramen ovale rather than the patent ductus arteriosus. [17]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- History and Physical
content: On physical examination, affected infants appear cyanotic. Respiratory distress may present as labored breathing with subcostal, suprasternal, and intercostal retractions related to underlying lung parenchymal disease. Infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia demonstrate a scaphoid abdomen on examination. In cases of sepsis, presentation may include refractory hypotension, multiorgan failure, and bleeding related to disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. [18]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Evaluation
content: Evaluation of an infant with suspected persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn includes obtaining blood gas, chest x-ray, and echocardiogram.
contents: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Evaluation. Evaluation of an infant with suspected persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn includes obtaining blood gas, chest x-ray, and echocardiogram.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: Sepsis should be ruled out with a complete blood count with differential and blood culture. If ECMO support is anticipated, coagulation studies and a head ultrasound should be performed before cannulation, if possible. Furthermore, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), a hormone produced by stressed right ventricles, may also indicate persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. BNP levels are elevated in babies with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. BNP level of more than 550 pg/mL is predictive of persistent pulmonary hypertension. [19]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: Arterial blood gas demonstrates low partial pressure of arterial oxygen (paO 2 ). In sepsis, leucocytosis or leucopenia may be seen. CRP may be high in sepsis. The following equation may calculate the oxygenation index: Oxygenation index (OI) = Mean airway pressure x FiO 2 x 100/PaO 2

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: An oxygenation index greater than 15, along with a preductal-postductal saturation difference of greater than 10%, is suggestive of high pulmonary vascular resistance. [18] . A persistent OI greater than 20, or an OI greater than 30, should prompt transfer to an ECMO-capable center; an OI of 40 often indicates an immediate need for ECMO.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Chest radiographs may show signs of underlying lung parenchymal disease.; however, echocardiography is the gold standard for confirming the diagnosis. Echocardiography is also used to follow therapeutic efficacy. The direction of flow across PDA and PFO, interventricular septal deviation or flattening, and regurgitation across the tricuspid valve (TR jet) are used to estimate right ventricular and pulmonary vascular pressure. The TR jet may be inaccurate in 30% of cases due to poor right ventricular function. Echocardiography also provides information about right and left ventricular function, which is vital in treating persistent pulmonary hypertension. [20] [15] Poor right ventricular function coupled with low right and left ventricular output is predictive of poor outcomes. [21]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Management Approaches
content: Management of persistent pulmonary hypertension includes maintaining temperature, glucose, cardiovascular support, and intravascular volume. [1] Treatment includes lung recruitment and vasopressor support, as well as pulmonary vasodilator therapy. Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) is the most studied agent in large randomized clinical trials and is the only FDA-approved vasodilator for persistent pulmonary hypertension in the United States.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Management Approaches
content: Past therapeutic interventions included hyperventilation, alkali infusion, sedation, paralysis, inotropes, and tolazoline, but most of these strategies are outdated and not being used anymore. The response to alkalosis induced by hyperventilation and alkali infusion is short-lived, and prolonged alkalosis can cause reactive hyperreactivity, worsening persistent pulmonary hypertension. [22] Alkalosis also causes cerebral vasoconstriction and may be associated with worse neurologic outcomes.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Inotropes
content: Ionotropic agents are often used in persistent pulmonary hypertension. Dopamine and milrinone are commonly used medications. Dopamine is a nonselective vasoconstrictor and should be used with caution in higher doses. [23] Increasing systemic blood pressure helps reduce extra-cardiac shunting across the PDA, although the optimal blood pressure values are not yet known.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation
content: The mainstay of treatment is improving oxygenation by optimizing mechanical ventilatory support. Gentle ventilation and maintaining adequate lung volume are essential management strategies in persistent pulmonary hypertension. Though oxygen is a potent vasodilator, fractional inspired oxygen concentration (FiO 2 ) over 50% is rarely beneficial. [24]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation
content: Achieving adequate lung volume improves oxygenation and pulmonary vascular resistance in newborns with parenchymal lung disease. A conventional or high-frequency ventilator can be used to correct any ventilation-perfusion mismatch. [25]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation
content: A preductal oxygen saturation target of 92% to 97% is generally optimal in late preterm and term babies. [26] However, each patient must be approached individually. In acute severe persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, targeting an oxygen saturation range of 93% to 98% can be beneficial, particularly when factors such as a pH less than 7.25, lactic acidosis, and ongoing therapeutic hypothermia are present. Also, with FiO 2 requirements below 0.6 and a lower risk of lung toxicity, a higher saturation target may be beneficial. Generally, saturation values between 99% and 100% should be avoided. [27]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Surfactant therapy
content: Studies show conflicting results with surfactant use in persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. In infants with parenchymal lung disease, surfactant use is associated with improved oxygenation in mild disease (oxygenation index 15-25). [28]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Surfactant therapy
content: The oxygenation index is used to assess disease severity. A persistent oxygenation index greater than 40 is often used to indicate severity and the need for ECMO. ECMO is life-saving but is invasive, labor-intensive, and associated with severe complications, eg, intracranial hemorrhage. [29]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Inhaled nitric oxide
content: INO causes selective pulmonary vasodilation and is the only FDA-approved pulmonary vasodilator therapy in neonates with persistent pulmonary hypertension. This agent is a rapid and potent vasodilator used in inhaled form. Treatment with iNO should always start at 20 ppm to assess response. Large trials showed the efficacy of iNO in decreasing the need for ECMO. [30] [31]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Inhaled nitric oxide
content: While iNO is the mainstay of treatment for persistent fetal circulation, it did not decrease mortality, hospital stay, or risk of neurologic impairment. Early initiation of iNO did not affect the need for ECMO or the risk of death or neurodevelopmental outcomes. [32] In the presence of severe left ventricular dysfunction or suboptimal management of severe parenchymal disease, iNO may not be effective. Clinical outcomes may improve with iNO when the oxygenation index is between 15 and 40. Optimal lung recruitment with careful avoidance of both atelectasis and hyperinflation, regardless of the type of mechanical ventilation, is essential to ensure adequate iNO delivery. [33] This treatment is rarely helpful in cases with an oxygenation index greater than 40, and aggressive measures, eg, ECMO, are essential to prevent death. [16]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Milrinone
content: Milrinone is an inotropic vasodilator that inhibits phosphodiesterase III, thereby improving right and left ventricular function and oxygenation in infants with severe pulmonary hypertension. [18] Furthermore, milrinone reduces systemic vascular and pulmonary venous pressure, thereby improving left ventricular performance. Therefore, this agent is typically used as adjunctive therapy to iNO. [34] However, milrinone is nonselective and can cause systemic hypotension, which may negatively affect myocardial perfusion and cardiac function. [35]

[18] Furthermore, milrinone reduces systemic vascular and pulmonary venous pressure, thereby improving left ventricular performance. Therefore, this agent is typically used as adjunctive therapy to iNO. [34] However, milrinone is nonselective and can cause systemic hypotension, which may negatively affect myocardial perfusion and cardiac function. [35]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Sildenafil
content: Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase V inhibitor. Although not yet approved by the FDA for the treatment of persistent fetal circulation, clinical data suggest that sildenafil is beneficial in infants who did not respond to iNO. It is usually administered orally since the intravenous form is rarely available. Studies have shown improved oxygenation with both oral and intravenous forms of sildenafil. [36] [37]

content: In low-resource settings where iNO is not available, oral sildenafil (1-2 mg/kg every 6 hours) is typically the initial treatment of choice. [38] Furthermore, a recent network meta-analysis reported encouraging results for the combination of oral sildenafil and intravenous milrinone in settings where iNO was not available. [39]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- Sedatives and antianxiolytics
content: Agitation can increase pulmonary vascular resistance and further worsen persistent pulmonary hypertension. Sedatives and antianxiolytic are used in infants with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn as adjunctive therapy to reduce wide swings in saturations. [40] These medications can be given as continuous infusions or as needed.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Treatment / Management -- ECMO
content: ECMO bypasses the heart and lungs, providing the time needed to resolve lung pathology. In severe respiratory failure, ECMO use was associated with improved survival. [41] The results of ECMO use in persistent pulmonary hypertension depend on the underlying etiology. The best outcomes in survival are seen in infants with meconium aspiration syndrome. ECMO use in other conditions, eg, trisomy 21 or congenital diaphragmatic hernia, has a morbidity following ECMO or a low survival rate of 1 year. Very few infants survived with no long-term sequelae (12%). [42] Although the use of this modality in persistent fetal circulation has drastically decreased since improved ventilation strategies and the introduction of iNO, it remains an effective rescue therapy.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnosis includes cyanotic congenital heart disease, which presents with cyanosis. iNO treatment worsens the clinical condition in total anomalous pulmonary venous return and should be avoided. Infants with PDA, transposition of great vessels, and coarctation of the aorta can present with differential cyanosis. [20]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Prognosis
content: Outcomes in persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn depend on the underlying etiology. Surviving infants with persistent pulmonary hypertension have long-term neurodevelopmental, cognitive, and hearing problems. [43] [44] [45] Approximately 1 in 4 infants with persistent pulmonary hypertension have neurodevelopmental delays and hearing impairment. The risk is higher in infants with underlying conditions, eg, congenital diaphragmatic hernia or genetic disorders.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Prognosis
content: In addition to the severity and etiology of persistent pulmonary hypertension in newborns, small for gestational age and Hispanic ethnicity are independent risk factors for higher mortality and morbidity in the first year after discharge. [9] Infants with mild disease are at higher risk for hospital readmission than term infants with no persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Complications
content: Complications of persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborns are related to the underlying cause. In meconium aspiration syndrome, air leaks, eg, pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum, occur very frequently due to the ball-valve phenomenon or the need for high ventilator settings. [46] In infants with profound hypoxemia, multiorgan dysfunction can manifest as oliguria and bleeding diathesis due to disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence and patient education for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn focus on risk reduction, early recognition, and informed parental involvement throughout the perinatal period. Prenatal counseling should address modifiable maternal risk factors, including smoking, medication exposures such as NSAIDs and SSRIs, glycemic control in diabetes, and management of hypertensive disorders and infections during pregnancy.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Education for families should emphasize the importance of timely prenatal care, reporting decreased fetal movement, and seeking prompt medical attention for respiratory distress or cyanosis after birth. In the NICU setting, clinicians should communicate clearly with caregivers regarding disease mechanisms, anticipated clinical course, monitoring strategies, and treatment options, including ventilatory support, pulmonary vasodilator therapy, and potential escalation to ECMO. Consistent education and anticipatory guidance help reduce diagnostic delays, minimize agitation-related hypoxemia through supportive handling, and promote shared decision-making, thereby supporting safer care and improved neonatal outcomes. Additionally, parents should be educated about the long-term effects of hypoxic injury on the neonatal brain. Follow-up therapies play a crucial role in improving outcomes in these infants. These infants have a higher risk of readmission, increased mortality, and morbidity in the first year of life. [9]

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: PPHN is a life-threatening condition that arises from failure of the normal cardiopulmonary transition after birth, leading to elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, reduced pulmonary blood flow, and right-to-left shunting. It can result from lung parenchymal disease, such as respiratory distress syndrome or meconium aspiration, or from an underdeveloped pulmonary vasculature in conditions such as congenital diaphragmatic hernia and small-for-gestational-age infants. Early recognition and rapid, evidence-based intervention are critical to improving survival and minimizing complications. Clinical assessment, diagnostic evaluation using echocardiography, calculation of the oxygenation index, and laboratory studies guide management, while interventions range from ventilatory optimization and pulmonary vasodilators to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe cases.

title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management requires an interprofessional approach. Physicians, neonatologists, and advanced practitioners lead assessment and therapeutic decisions, while nurses monitor vital signs, identify cyanosis, and provide parent education. Respiratory therapists manage ventilatory support, initiate inhaled nitric oxide, and monitor treatment response. Pharmacists optimize medication safety and dosing, including pulmonary vasodilators and inotropes, while cardiologists and echocardiography technicians assess cardiac function and guide therapy. Surgeons and ECMO specialists intervene in critical cases, and radiologists help identify underlying pathology. Rehabilitation therapists, including speech, occupational, and physical therapists, contribute to long-term neurologic outcomes. Coordination, communication, and shared decision-making across this team enhance patient-centered care, safety, and overall outcomes. [43]
